Missouri passed a law to compensate the wrongfully convicted. Now it doesn’t want to pay.
Two men are seeking $2.4 million for their combined 38 years lost in prison. The attorney general is fighting them in court.
Dale Helmig is seeking compensation for the more than 14 years he spent wrongfully incarcerated in Missouri (Katie Moore/Marshall Project).
After Missouri lawmakers expanded eligibility for wrongfully convicted people to receive compensation last year, Dale Helmig thought he could get nearly $1 million for the more than 14 years he spent in prison. And Darryl Burton hoped to obtain more than $1.5 million for the 24-plus years he was incarcerated.
But today, they are back in the legal system that put them away. The state attorney general is arguing in court that the two men aren’t innocent, setting aside judges’ prior decisions — and that even if they were, the new law isn’t retroactive.
Missouri Attorney General Catherine Hanaway’s effort to fight their compensation requests — the first two under the new compensation law — is part of a long history of the office vigorously opposing innocence claims. Under her predecessors, attorneys there have kept people in prison even after a judge has ordered their release and continued to fight cases in the face of overwhelming evidence of innocence.
Peter Joy, a law professor at Washington University in St. Louis, said the Attorney General’s Office “has opposed claims of innocence on a very consistent basis, even though there have been times when the local prosecutor’s offices have recognized that the person had a valid claim of innocence.”
That doesn’t necessarily mean they aren’t examining each case on its merits, Joy said. But if they were opposing these without a “good faith basis,” it would be a violation of prosecutors’ ethical obligation to seek justice, he said. A spokesperson for Hanaway declined to comment, citing the pending cases.
When Helmig and Burton were released from prison, only those exonerated through DNA evidence qualified for state compensation — not people like them, whose convictions were overturned based on recantations or other types of newly discovered evidence.
Then, last year, the Missouri legislature expanded eligibility and increased the amount of money exonerees can collect. The measure was approved by Gov. Mike Kehoe.
The law allocates about $65,000 for every year of wrongful incarceration. That amount is paid on an annual basis, not as a lump sum.
In Helmig’s case, a judge in DeKalb County, about an hour north of Kansas City, ruled in 2010 that there was clear and convincing evidence that he was innocent.
Helmig had been convicted in the 1993 murder of his mother, Norma, whose body was found in a river in central Missouri, near where she lived. Prosecutors said his motive was a dispute over a phone bill, and that he’d thrown her purse from the bridge he would have traveled on from her home on the night of the murder.
But uncovered evidence implicated Helmig’s father, court records show. The couple were in divorce proceedings. Helmig’s father had access to her mail at a local post office, including a canceled check that was dated after her death and later found in the purse. That undermined the prosecution’s theory about when the purse had been discarded — a key detail in their case against Helmig.
A state trooper also recanted his testimony. During the trial, he had told jurors that Helmig had not denied killing his mother when, in fact, he had.

Burnout among Missouri’s doctors, lawyers and executives rarely announces itself. It shows up as a surgeon in Kansas City who stops sleeping through the night, a litigator in Clayton who adds a second drink most evenings, a hospital administrator in Springfield who snaps at a staff meeting and spends the drive home replaying it. Their work stays excellent. That is exactly the problem.
I am a licensed clinical social worker, and the people I see most often in this situation are not short on money, insurance or information. They are short on one thing: a way to get help that nobody at work will ever hear about.
The research on attorneys makes that point more clearly than anything else I know. The largest study of lawyer mental health, published in the Journal of Addiction Medicine in 2016, screened 12,825 licensed, employed attorneys. When the authors asked why people had not sought help, the two most common answers were not wanting others to find out and concerns about privacy or confidentiality. Among attorneys who had been in treatment, about half named the first reason.
That finding has held up. A 2026 research paper by my firm, CEREVITY, works through the decade of studies that followed and notes that the headline numbers vary with the method used. The fear of exposure is the one finding that shows up every time someone asks the question, in attorneys and in law students alike.
Doctors and senior executives carry the same calculation. A physician wonders who at the hospital will see the claim. A chief financial officer pictures the board hearing about it. A partner thinks about origination credit and what the firm did the last time someone admitted they were struggling. Each person decides, usually quickly and usually alone, that the safer move is to wait.
Here is what that waiting looks like in practice, in a composite drawn from common patterns rather than any one person. A Kansas City executive notices in January that she is lying awake at 3 a.m. By spring she is canceling lunches and rereading emails four times before sending them. By late summer a colleague asks if she is OK, and she says she is just busy. She finally calls someone in the fall, after a panic attack in a parking garage. The care she gets then is harder and slower than it would have been in January.
Missouri already has a piece of the answer, and it deserves more attention. The Missouri Bar’s lawyers’ assistance program offers counseling and referrals to every lawyer and judge in the state at no cost, and the Bar states plainly that its services are confidential and that reaching out does not affect a lawyer’s license. That last sentence matters more than any brochure. It answers the exact question that keeps people away.
Three changes would extend that logic beyond the bar.
First, employers should say the confidentiality promise out loud, in writing and from the top. A benefit nobody trusts is a benefit nobody uses. If a hospital system, law firm or company in St. Louis or Kansas City offers counseling, its leaders should spell out who can see what, and who cannot.

The pace of price increases stepped up in September, keeping inflation well above the Federal Reserve's target, while the economy grew faster than expected in the third quarter, according to Commerce Department reports Thursday.
The personal consumption expenditures price index increased a seasonally adjusted 0.5% for the month, putting the annual inflation rate at 3.6%.The monthly increase was in line with the Dow Jones consensus, while the annual rate was 0.1 percentage point below.
Excluding food and energy, core PCE posted respective readings of 0.3% and 3.1%, in line with the consensus. While the Fed follows both measures closely, officials generally see the core reading as more indicative of longer-term inflation trends.
While inflation continued to run ahead of the Fed's 2% target, the Commerce Department also reported that gross domestic product was strong in the third quarter.
GDP increased at a seasonally adjusted annualized pace of 3.4%, better than the 3.1% estimate and well ahead of the 2.2% in the second quarter.
Also, consumer spending proved resilient, increasing 0.5% a bit below the forecast for a 0.6% gain, while personal income rose 0.2%, compared to the forecast for 0.3%.
The reports come the day after the Fed voted to hold its benchmark interest rate in a range between 3.75%-4%. Despite elevated inflation readings, central bank officials insist they can afford to evaluate incoming data before deciding on their next move.
"The period right in front of us is information rich. There is a lot that's happening in the world. My colleagues and I are keen to take notice of it," Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said.
However, the data deluge from Thursday shows the Fed could have more work to do.
A Labor Department report also released Thursday showed that layoffs remain low. Initial jobless claims edged lower to a seasonally adjusted 194,000 for the week ending Oct. 24, below the estimate for 200,000 and near levels last seen in the late 1960s.
Stock market futures were negative following the releases while Treasury yields also fell.
Economic growth has been driven by higher levels of investment during the artificial intelligence buildout, as well as high levels of consumer and government spending.
Consumer spending rose 3.8% in the third quarter, the same pace as the prior period. Gross private domestic investment soared 19.4%, driven by a 20.9% surge in equipment spending and an 8.4% jump on intellectual property products.
Real sales to private domestic purchasers, a proxy that Fed officials use for underlying demand, rose 4.9%, compared to a 4.6% increase in the second quarter.
There was some good inflation news for the period: On a quarterly basis, PCE prices rose 2.1% on the headline number and 2.5% for core, down respectively from 5% and 3.3% in Q2.

European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde will step down on Feb. 7 next year, she announced Thursday, formally kicking off a succession race that will be shaped by political bargaining and France's looming fiscal crisis.
Lagarde has led the central bank since July 2019, steering its responses to the Covid-19 pandemic, the Russia-Ukraine war and a series of energy price shocks that sent inflation in the European Union above 11% in 2022 and spurred the end of the post-Financial Crisis era of negative interest rates.
Lagarde will depart nearly nine months before her term was due to expire in October 2027, while the process to appoint her successor will begin immediately.
What the ECB is looking for in a successor
Senior ECB figures are already in talks about filling other senior roles, with chief economist Philip Lane and influential executive board member Isabel Schnabel, responsible for market operations, also due to step down next year.
The ECB is institutionally independent, and its Governing Council comprises the six-member Executive Board and the governors of the 21 euro area national central banks.
But appointments to its top jobs are made by the European Council following consultations with the European Parliament and euro area member states, with negotiations generally reflecting political bargaining over national representation and influence.
Spain's Pablo Hernández de Cos and the Netherlands' Klaas Knot, who both led their respective central banks for recent stints, are widely regarded as top contenders to replace Lagarde.
De Cos served from 2018 to 2024 and is now general manager of the Bank for International Settlements. Knot was Dutch central bank chief from 2011 until 2025 and is a distinguished visiting fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics.
The appointment of a new president is seen as crucial amid market debate over whether the ECB could use one of its intervention mechanisms as France faces a mounting sovereign debt crisis.
France's presidential election, due next year, is injecting further uncertainty as the country's bond yields spike and its spread over euro area benchmark Germany's rises to the highest level since the bloc's Sovereign Debt Crisis of the early 2010s.
Berenberg Chief Economist Holger Schmieding said that as a result, the ECB would need to consider who was best placed to deal with potential financial turbulence.
"As a former chair of the G20's Financial Stability Board (FSB), Knot may have an edge in this respect," Schmieding said in a note.

It’s awards season, and while the Cardinals’ 2026 campaign was an unconventional one by their standards -- one that focused on young players with designs on the future -- it’s still one that featured its fair share of awards candidates.
So before we reach November, here is a look at the Cardinals’ top awards candidates.
Gold Glove Awards
Winners announced Sunday
The Cardinals have three finalists: second baseman JJ Wetherholt, shortstop Masyn Winn and pitcher Michael McGreevy.
McGreevy was a surprise contender, but he shouldn’t have been. The Cardinals raved about his defensive ability all year, and his glove is seen as a real contributing factor to his success on the mound, which included a roughly league-average 3.95 ERA despite a strikeout rate that ranked in just the ninth percentile. McGreevy’s 5 Defensive Runs Saved put him in a tie for second among all pitchers behind, oddly, Braves reliever Brent Suter. McGreevy would be an unlikely winner, though, if just because of name recognition: His competitors are the Braves’ Chris Sale and the Mets’ Nolan McLean.
Wetherholt and Winn as finalists were much less surprising. Winn won a Gold Glove in 2025, and he was first among National League shortstops again in DRS and Statcast’s Outs Above Average (OAA) in 2026. Winn is up against the Diamondbacks’ Geraldo Perdomo and the Cubs’ Dansby Swanson, and he’s probably the favorite to win it again. If so, he’ll only have … 11 to go to catch Ozzie Smith.
Wetherholt might be even more deserving. He was in the 100th percentile in OAA and Statcast’s fielding run value, and some metrics had him as the best defender in baseball. One of those metrics, however, is not DRS, where he’s tied for second among NL second basemen, behind the Brewers’ Brice Turang, one of his competitors for this award (along with the Pirates’ Brandon Lowe). Turang has already won one Gold Glove, and, considering his importance to the Brewers’ success this year, one might consider him the favorite to do it again. If Wetherholt wins this, there’s no question it will be the first of many.
Rookie of the Year Award
Finalists announced Monday, winners Nov. 9
For most of the year, Wetherholt was considered the favorite for this award, but his bat faded down the stretch, including a .307 OBP after the All-Star break. That allowed the Reds’ Sal Stewart and the Mets’ McLean and Carson Benge to gain on him and, arguably, pass him.
Still, there’s a great statistical case to be made for Wetherholt. Along with the Cubs’ Pete Crow-Armstrong, he might have been the best defensive player in the sport this year (at least by Outs Above Average). Wetherholt’s WAR lead over Stewart is dramatic: 4.6 to 2.0, according to FanGraphs. Wetherholt’s offensive numbers were suppressed by his home park, while Stewart’s, fair to say, were not. Stewart’s baseball-card numbers might end up earning him the nod, but even with the second-half fade, it’s hard to argue Wetherholt doesn’t deserve serious consideration.

1. Net interest income: When it comes right down to it, banks' core business is charging interest on loaned money they borrowed themselves. The difference between a bank's internal cost of borrowed capital and the interest it's collecting from its loan customers is net interest income, or NII. Jim Cramer told Mad Money viewers to swap Exxon for Chevron, and on October 30 both giants report back to back. Six numbers will reveal whether that call holds or collapses.

“I think Exxon’s good. I think Chevron’s better. I would make that swap unless you have some tax implications. CVX is a better way to go,” Cramer said. This year, the two stocks have moved almost in tandem. Exxon is up 48.4% year to date, and Chevron is up 47.0%.
Chevron Absorbed the Middle East Shock Better

Chevron CFO Eimear Bonner reported adjusted EPS of $6.06 and adjusted free cash flow (the cash left over after capital spending) of $15.4 billion, with only about 1% of production affected by the conflict. Mike Wirth, who spoke as chair and CEO, cited record U.S. upstream output of nearly 2.1 million barrels of oil equivalent per day and $3 billion in structural cost cuts reached six months early. “Amid geopolitical uncertainty and market volatility, Chevron delivered a strong second quarter,” Wirth said.

- Whether the lost Middle East production has come back
- When Guyana’s fifth FPSO (a floating production, storage, and offloading vessel) starts up
- How chemical and refining margins held up

Key points
Bank of America's Holiday Spending Survey finds early to mid-December may surpass Black Friday as the most popular time for holiday shopping.

CHARLOTTE, N.C., Oct. 29, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Black Friday traditionally marks the unofficial start of the holiday shopping season, however this year consumers are planning to make their biggest holiday shopping push a little later. According to the Bank of America 2026 Holiday Spending Survey, 29% of consumers plan to do most of their holiday shopping in early to mid-December, up from 19% in 2025. Meanwhile, those planning to concentrate most of their shopping around Black Friday fell from 25% to 17%.
Fewer than two out of five (38%) consumers said they have shopped or will shop earlier in 2026, down from 52% in 2025. However, sentiment is running cooler than spending — Bank of America Institute's latest Consumer Checkpoint shows holiday spending is already increasing at a solid rate through September.
"Consumers are being more deliberate this year, from setting their own timelines to staying focused on their budgets," said Mary Hines Droesch, Head of Consumer and Small Business Products and Analytics at Bank of America. "At the same time, our Bank of America spending data shows the season is off to a healthy start."
Budgets hold steady, and shoppers look inward Nearly half of consumers (48%) expect to spend about the same this holiday season as last year – up from 39% in 2025, with 39% also saying they will spend less on holiday gifts this year – down from 42% in 2025. Meanwhile, only 12% plan to spend more, down from 19% last year. Nearly two-thirds (63%) base holiday spending strictly on their own budget rather than what friends or family spend, rising to 78% of baby boomers.
Consumers' top strategies for avoiding overspending include:
Shopping during sales events (30%).
Setting a firm per-person spending limit (27%).
Using credit card rewards, points, or cash back (21%).

Nearly three-quarters of consumers (72%) do not plan to use AI tools for holiday shopping, up from 49% in 2025.
14% of consumers plan to buy gifts directly through social media, down from 35% in 2025 – with the sharpest drops among younger generations.
62% say viral content has no effect on their shopping decisions.

Phishing emails posing as retailers (18%)

Too good to be true deals on gifts or services (16%)

A Cole County Circuit Court judge ruled Thursday that a state law allowing charter schools to operate in Boone County is not an unconstitutional special law (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent).
A 2024 law that allowed charter schools to open in Boone County is not an unconstitutional “special law,” a Cole County judge ruled Thursday.
Columbia Public Schools challenged the statute, arguing that it violated the Missouri Constitution’s prohibition on special laws, which single out localities or people when a general law could apply.

Missouri marijuana businesses had reason to celebrate in April when the federal officials moved medical marijuana into a less restrictive category of controlled substances.
The federal order could also set marijuana companies on a path to substantial federal tax savings. For years, federal law has prevented many cannabis businesses from deducting ordinary expenses — including employee salaries, rent and other costs — when calculating their federal taxes.
But months after the change, Missouri businesses still don’t know exactly how to claim those savings, especially if they sell both medical and recreational marijuana.
That uncertainty was a key topic this month on the Missouri Division of Cannabis Regulation’s DCR OutLoud podcast, where leaders of the Missouri Cannabis Trade Association said they’re waiting for federal tax officials to explain how the new rules will work.
“Not only is the cannabis industry here in Missouri one of the most regulated industries, but it’s also one of the most taxed,” said Andrew Mullins, executive director of the association.
The federal tax rule at the center of the debate is known as Section 280E. It generally prevents businesses that sell certain federally prohibited drugs from deducting everyday business expenses. This prohibition results in an effective income tax rate on marijuana businesses of as high as 80%, compared to the standard federal corporate rate of 21%.
Missouri already allows licensed marijuana businesses to deduct those expenses on their state income tax returns, but the federal restriction has remained in place.
The April order moved marijuana regulated under state medical licenses into Schedule III but left recreational marijuana in Schedule I. That leaves businesses that sell both types of cannabis with a difficult question: How much of their spending can they deduct?
“Certainly they’re all very anxious to see if relief is on the way and if we’re going to see that guidance from the IRS that basically directs what they can do…” Mullins said.

“In our state, the difference between medical and just adult-use consumer product really only comes into play at that moment of sale when a particular tax rate is applied,” Moore said on the podcast. “But that [Department of Justice] order seems to be really organized around medical marijuana.”

Specs
From a distance, the Apex follows the same general design as the Alphafly models before it: an airy mesh upper over a thick foam midsole with a carbon fiber plate and Zoom Air units in the forefoot. But the Apex has some major updates compared to its forebears. The other big change? The Apex is a zero-drop shoe, measuring an even 40mm across at both the heel and forefoot. No other super shoe on the market has a zero-drop platform; even Altra, a brand famous for its zero-drop models, gave its top-tier racer a 4mm drop. This is a milestone year for the New York City Marathon: Sunday’s race will be the 50th anniversary of the five-borough course, which was first run in 1976.
From its inaugural year in 1970, the race was held in Central Park. But five men—Ted Corbitt, Fred Lebow, George Spitz, Percy Sutton, and George Hirsch—spearheaded an effort to change the course to run through each of the city’s five boroughs, starting in Staten Island and ending in Manhattan.
Only one of the “trailblazers,” as the New York Road Runners calls them, is still alive. At 92, George Hirsch has seen the NYC Marathon develop from a fringe race in Central Park to the largest marathon in the world. A longtime magazine publisher (including at Runner’s World), Hirsch was the chairman of the NYRR board of directors from 2004 to 2023, and he helped generate the initial media buzz and funds for the 1976 race.
In an interview in mid-October, Hirsch shared his memories of the early days of the five-borough race and reflected on how it’s evolved over a half century.
A troubled city
The mid-1970s were a tough time to live in New York City. Crime was high, the economy was struggling, and thousands of residents fled for the suburbs. The city needed a pick-me-up, according to Hirsch. When Hirsch first heard the idea for a multi-borough race from Corbitt and Spitz, his immediate thought was that it would be a massive undertaking. Bridges would need to be closed, police hired, funds raised.
“Closing down a major city, the largest city in the United States, for a foot race was ambitious and it was unheard of at the time,” he said, noting that the Boston Marathon has a smaller footprint on the city proper. Still, the pioneers were able to secure the backing of the mayor, Abe Beame, although it was not pitched as a recurring event.
Now, they just needed to execute their idea. “Going into the [1976 race], our little running community was super excited about this New York Marathon,” Hirsch said. “But what we had no way of knowing was how the city was going to embrace it.”
So how did it go?
When Hirsch lined up on the Verrazano-Narrows Bridge in Staten Island in 1976, he was eager but a little nervous. That quickly changed, as he descended the bridge into Brooklyn.
“All of a sudden, there were crowds on both sides of the street yelling and cheering,” he remembered. “Sure, the crowds were nothing like they are today. Don’t misunderstand me. But by those days’ standards, it was extraordinary. And that was the way it was for our entire run.”
Hirsch ran 2:49:29 that day, placing 156th out of 1,539 finishers. Bill Rodgers won the men’s race, and Miki Gorman was the top woman. The atmosphere after the race was electric. Hirsch threw a party at his brownstone that night.
“It was clearly a victory party,” he said. “There was no question. It was a big celebration. We knew it had worked … It didn’t have to work. There’s a lot of things that can go wrong. And this one, it didn’t happen. It just worked. It was terrific, and we felt really great about it.”
The legacy of the marathon
After the success of the first year, the marathon began to steadily grow, and the five-borough format was adopted permanently. By 1980, there were 12,512 finishers. A decade later, there were 23,774. The race broke 40,000 finishers in 2009, and now it’s routinely one of the largest marathons in the world. Sunday’s race could see a record 60,000 participants.

We’ve all been there: You head out for an easy run and settle into your usual pace, but after a mile or two, your breathing feels labored and you notice your heart rate climbing higher than normal. However, you’re still going at your usual pace on your usual route, so what gives?
If you judge the run by pace alone, you might see no reason to change anything. But those other signals suggest you’re paying a higher price than usual to hold that speed.
Of course, you probably already know that factors like heat, hills, fatigue, and stress can make your usual pace feel harder. But with so much advice about what to pay attention to during a run, it can be tough to know which signals to trust and how to use them to evaluate your effort.
And without a clear way to interpret those signals, you might inadvertently push too hard on an easy day or miss the intended effort during a speed workout. Repeat these mistakes, and over time, you can disrupt the balance between training and recovery, making it harder to build the fitness you need to race your best.
The solution: A system from ultramarathon runner and endurance coach Nick Farr, head coach and founder of P3 Fitness. Farr organizes running feedback into three categories—performance output, biological load, and subjective feedback—and uses them together to understand how a run is unfolding.
Here’s how to use Farr’s three-category system to make every run count, build fitness more consistently, and arrive on race day ready to perform your best.
Why Your Run Data Needs Context
“No single metric tells you the whole story [of a run],” Farr says. For example, your pace tells you how fast you ran. But, inherently, it can’t tell you how difficult that pace felt or how your body responded to that pace.
To get a fuller picture, Farr separates training feedback into three categories, each of which answers one of those three questions:
- Performance output: What work are you doing?
- Biological load: How is your body responding to that work?
- Subjective feedback: How does the effort feel?
Evaluating the answers to these questions in concert with one another helps Farr and his athletes understand whether a run matches its intended purpose. It also gives runners a way to recognize when environmental conditions, fatigue, or other factors might call for an adjustment.
Performance Output: Shows What You’re Doing
Performance output describes the work you produce during a run. Metrics like pace, speed, distance, time, elevation, cadence, stride length, and power fall into this category, Farr says.
These metrics help you track what you accomplish. They show how quickly you covered a route, how far you ran, or how much climbing you tackled. You can also compare output across runs to see how your performance changes over time.
But output alone offers an incomplete view of the effort. You might finish an easy run at your usual pace, even though heat, hills, or fatigue made it much harder than normal. If you focus only on the pace number, you could miss the signs that you pushed beyond the effort you intended.
Biological Load: Reveals How Your Body Responds to Effort
Biological load, which Farr also calls internal or physiological load, describes how your body responds to the work you’re doing. Numbers such as heart rate, breathing rate, oxygen consumption, and core temperature can all offer information about your body’s response to a certain pace, environment, or training block.

Adobe (ADBE -0.66%) stock hit its closing record of $688.37 on Nov. 19, 2021. Almost five years later, shares of the creative software company trade around $248 as I write this -- about 64% off that high. And at their June 25 closing low of $193.41, they were down about 72%, the stock's deepest drop since the dot-com crash.
Deep drops are nothing new to Adobe, though. Using daily closing prices since 1990 (adjusted for stock splits, with dividends left out), the stock had fallen at least 30% from a record close eight times before this slide. It then set a new record after every one.
But I don't think that history settles much, because the two slumps this one most resembles started with a problem today's Adobe doesn't have.
Image source: Getty Images.
The slow comebacks took around six years
Six of the eight drops came in the 1990s, and they were deep, running from about 31% to 66%. But they were also mostly short.
Five of the six went from one record close to the next in around 18 months or less. The longest, which bottomed in August 1998, took about 3.4 years.
The two drops after that were another story. After peaking on Nov. 6, 2000, Adobe stock lost around 80% by August 2002, and it didn't close at a new record until Nov. 16, 2006.
The next slump, from an Oct. 24, 2007, peak, cut the stock around 67% by March 2009. Its next record was on July 12, 2013, about 5.7 years after the 2007 high.
Both times, the climb from the bottom back to the old high took over four years by itself. Today's slump is almost five years old, and as of this writing, the stock would have to gain around 177% to get back to its record.
In 2002 and 2009, the business shrank first
In the first of those long slumps, Adobe's revenue shrank two straight years, from fiscal 2000's $1.27 billion to $1.16 billion by fiscal 2002. Net income fell around a third over the same stretch.
Then sales turned. Revenue climbed 11% in fiscal 2003 and accelerated to 29% growth in fiscal 2004, so investors who hung on could see the rebound in the numbers.
The 2008-2009 recession cut deeper. Fiscal 2009 revenue slid 18%, to around $2.9 billion.
Interestingly, the stock's 2013 record was in a year when revenue fell 8%. Adobe had stopped new releases of its Creative Suite software, which customers bought outright, to focus on Creative Cloud subscriptions, which spread out revenue over time. Investors pushed the stock to a record before the new model's sales caught up.
Is this time different?
In one big way, it is: Adobe's business never shrank this time. Management expects fiscal 2026 revenue of around $26.6 billion, about 69% above the $15.8 billion it pulled in during fiscal 2021 -- the year the stock peaked.
Adobe's revenue climbed 13% year over year in its fiscal third quarter of 2026 (the period ending Aug. 28, 2026), hitting a quarterly record of $6.76 billion. Its non-GAAP (adjusted) earnings per share climbed even faster, up 15%.
The worry is what's next. Investors fear that artificial intelligence (AI) agents might take over tasks people now do with software like Adobe's, which bills subscribers per user, or seat.
If fewer people need a seat, Adobe's recurring revenue could shrink. That arguably makes this slump tougher to ride out than the past two. In 2002 and 2009, a sales recovery could show the hit was temporary. Now, Adobe needs to show that AI adds more to its business than it takes away.

Don't blame Intel's (INTC) weak guidance, tied to a prolonged memory chip supply shortage, for the fresh rout on tech stocks.
Blame the hyperscalers like Amazon (AMZN), Alphabet (GOOGL) and Meta (META) for not guiding Wall Street properly on how much they intended to spend this year and next on AI infrastructure. The bills are coming in much larger than expected, and Wall Street can't stomach it.
That's why you aren't seeing many heroes out there saying buy the dip right now. That's why Friday is shaping up to be another bloodbath for tech stocks.
Remember, it's cash flow that will be used to repay all the debt hyperscalers are poised to incur to support their robust AI infrastructure buildouts. The fact that cash flow is drying up because of a protracted period of spending is the bug causing the debt and stock markets to catch a cold.
Kudos to Amazon for at least not burying its free cash flow metric, the most important metric for tech at the moment, at the bottom of its earnings release. It made it no less tough to stomach, but at least it was easy to find quickly.
Amazon's free cash flow decreased to an outflow of $42.4 billion for the trailing twelve months, driven primarily by a year-over-year increase of $94.8 billion in purchases of property and equipment. This increase primarily reflects investments in artificial intelligence, Amazon said.

Medicaid recipients who are disabled or have a chronic illness will not have to prove they are unable to work to be exempted from new work requirements that take effect next year, a federal judge ruled Thursday.
The decision by U.S. District Judge Richard Stearns in Boston grants a partial victory to the 25 Democratic-led states that sued the Trump administration in June, arguing that its new “medically frail” designation was too narrow and would make it too difficult for ill and disabled people to remain on Medicaid, the joint federal-state health insurance program for people with low incomes.
However, the decision also granted some concessions to the administration, most notably by allowing the new work requirements included in the measure known as the One Big Beautiful Big Act to remain in place.
Under that broad 2025 tax and spending law, states that have expanded Medicaid to cover more adults under the Affordable Care Act must require enrollees to work, go to school or volunteer for at least 80 hours a month.
In addition to the 40 states (plus the District of Columbia) that have expanded Medicaid under the ACA, the new rules will apply to Georgia, Tennessee and Wisconsin, which have used federal waivers to expand their Medicaid programs.
In June, the Trump administration released interim guidelines stating that in order to qualify for a “medically frail” exception to the work rules, a Medicaid recipient had to have a significant condition and be significantly impaired in their ability to work.
In a statement unveiling the new guidance, Dr. Mehmet Oz, director of the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, said it would help Medicaid enrollees “build skills and independence through work, education, job training, or community service, creating new opportunities for themselves and their families.”

Judge rejects constitutional challenge to Missouri property tax caps tied to stadium bill
Cole County judge rules taxpayers, school districts and counties lack standing to sue, rejecting claims that the law unfairly treats different counties
Cole County Circuit Judge Christopher Limbaugh ruled that property tax caps included in a bill to support professional sports stadiums are constitutional(Anna Spoerre/Missouri Independent).
A Cole County judge on Wednesday rejected a constitutional challenge to property tax caps lawmakers added to a bill aimed at keeping the Kansas City Chiefs in Missouri.
The caps, structured as credits against property tax bills, applied to 97 of Missouri’s 114 counties. The caps, voted on in April, will mean this year’s property tax bill cannot be higher than last year in up to 22 counties, and cannot increase more than 5% in 75 others.
Of the 97 counties listed in the legislation, 61 passed it, 14 designated for tax bill freezes and 47 with the 5% cap; 12 counties rejected it; and 23 counties did not hold elections.
The law was challenged by two individuals, six school districts and one fire district. Forty-three counties, as well as individual county commissioners, later joined the case.
In his decision, Cole County Circuit Judge Christopher Limbaugh ruled that none of the plaintiffs had the right to sue and that they were wrong on the legal issues they raised.
Individuals do not have a right to sue simply because they believe they are at a disadvantage to a person in another county because of a property tax law, Limbaugh wrote. And the taxing districts can’t sue because they haven’t lost any money, he ruled.
The counties didn’t have the right to sue either, he wrote. They can’t raise issues on behalf of the school districts and other agencies they collect money for, he ruled.
“Missouri case law does not recognize standing based on dissatisfaction that other jurisdictions may impose different local taxes or conduct assessments differently; rather, Missouri case law recognizes standing where the plaintiff can show a present, direct adverse effect,” Limbaugh wrote.
The lawsuit was filed in September 2025, challenging the right of the legislature to write a law that provided property tax freezes in some counties, caps in others and no limits on increases in individual bills in 17 other counties and the city of St. Louis. The lawsuit alleged lawmakers used population and other characteristics to single out individual counties, creating special or local laws prohibited by the Missouri Constitution.
It was the second case challenging the stadium bill passed in a June 2025 special session. On Sept. 1, the Missouri Supreme Court heard an appeal in a separate lawsuit filed by two lawmakers and a conservative activist.
The court must decide whether state Sen. Mike Moon, an Ash Grove Republican, state Rep. Bryant Wolfin, a Ste. Genevieve Republican, and conservative activist Ron Calzone have standing. In January, Limbaugh ruled they did not and dismissed their lawsuit.
If the court finds Moon, Wolfin and Calzone do have standing, their case returns to Limbaugh.

This makes sense to anyone who follows James on Instagram, where he’s shared videos eating a $225 bagel, housing a five-pound hot dog, and spending a month eating nothing but pasta and gelato. While James is perhaps best known for appearing on reality TV shows like The Bachelor and Dancing With the Stars, he’s now built a social media following of like-minded runners/eaters.
James’s marathon and carb-loading journeys actually predate his time as a celebrity. He raced his first marathon in Chicago in 2019, and has run a dozen since. On November 1, he’ll line up for his sixth consecutive New York City Marathon, but this time, he’s more focused on eating than on his time.
“I’ve got a lot of eating planned,” he says. “I’m going to a family-style dinner at Little Ruby’s on Thursday. It’s probably my favorite restaurant in the city. I eat there all the time. Then, I’ll go to Lavagna and have pasta Friday.”
In fact, James takes his marathon-week dining so seriously, he’s partnered with Yelp to create a marathon weekend dining guide for out-of-towners. The list, which includes Melba’s Restaurant, Chrissy’s Pizza, and Winson Bakery, looks beyond the typical tourist fare in Manhattan to give marathon runners a true tour of New York’s best food.
James’s fueling expertise is hard-won. He ran his second NYC Marathon in 2022 alongside former NYC Marathon winner Shalane Flanagan. On race day, he ambitiously told her he was trying to run a sub-three-hour marathon, despite not training properly for the task.
“I just hit the wall,” he remembers. “We’re walking up First Avenue, and I’m like, ‘Oh my gosh, I have 10 more miles to walk with a former marathon champion.’” While he tried to send Flanagan on ahead, she stuck by him and coached him to a 3:46:45.
“Running with her inspired me to take the sport seriously,” he says. “It’s really been a complete lifestyle change after that in terms of getting adequate miles and workouts in. Then when it comes to race day, it’s a celebration and not a death march.”
When the two reunited at the same race in 2023, he finished in 3:04:50.

It’s a frigid Friday night in February in small-town Utah, and Conner Mantz and his wife, Kylie, are doing what they do pretty much every night: padding around in sweats, making pasta, talking. Apparently, there is a crack in the ceiling of the couple’s new house. I don’t see it, but luckily, Kylie did, mere days before the one-year warranty on their four-bedroom, 4,500-square-foot new build in a master-planned community runs out.

Adobe (ADBE) shares have lost 55.1% since their December 6, 2024 high, and that fall is the reason to look again. Adobe’s free cash flow over the last four quarters equaled 10.8% of its market value at the October 29 close, compared with 4.2% for the median S&P 500 company. Cash that plentiful for the price means a sound business on sale or one the market expects to shrink, so which is Adobe?
Adobe’s Free Cash Flow Is Still Rising
Adobe generated $10.6 billion in free cash flow, the cash left after running the business and paying for equipment, during the four quarters to August 28, 2026. This was up from $9.6 billion a year earlier. Like profit, this cash belongs to shareholders whether Adobe pays it out or not. Over time, a company’s share price tends to rise alongside the cash it produces for owners, especially when that figure is growing.
Subscriptions generate this cash, making up $6.56 billion of Adobe’s $6.76 billion revenue in fiscal Q3 2026. Revenue rose 12.0% over the last twelve months, following a 10.7% increase the year before. Equipment took 2.0% of its cash from operations over those twelve months, showing Adobe spends little to stay in business. The company keeps a large share of each sale as profit, recording an operating margin of 35.7% against 18.5% for the S&P 500.
Adobe owed $6.76 billion on August 28, 2026, while holding $5.64 billion in cash and short-term investments. The company paid a $0.26 billion interest bill over the last twelve months, against $9.27 billion of operating profit. Looking solely at these accounts, Adobe resembles a growing business priced cheaply rather than one in decline.
Why Investors Pay So Little For Adobe’s Cash
Investors may worry that Adobe’s growth will fade as AI changes software. Leadership is also changing: the shares fell 6.7% on September 4, 2026, after Adobe named Anil Chakravarthy as its next CEO, starting December 1. During its September 10, 2026 call, management itself said every software-as-a-service company will go through a shift to AI agents.

CCH Connections 2026 main-stage panel explored agentic AI, talent development, trust, and the priorities firm leaders should set for the next year
ORLANDO, Fla., October 30, 2026--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Wolters Kluwer Tax & Accounting brought together leaders from Microsoft, Salesforce, McKinsey, and Sandra Wiley Strategies at CCH Connections 2026 with a clear message for accounting firms: as AI agents move from recommending actions to taking them, the time to decide how work gets done, how trust is earned, and how people build expertise is now. The main-stage panel, The New Blueprint: Building the Future-Ready Firm, moderated by Matt Linderman, Partner at McKinsey, drew on what each leader has learned from adopting and scaling AI.
On Wednesday, panelists urged firms not to wait for a perfect firmwide AI strategy. Start with one workflow, secure the data behind it, and build agentic workflows with the governance and controls to deliver the intended outcomes. The session closed with a challenge for every firm leader: set priorities for the next 12 months and choose one practical move to make in the next 90 days.
"The future-ready firm will not be defined by technology alone. It will be defined by how leaders combine technology with trusted expertise, sound judgment, strong relationships, and a clear understanding of the outcomes their clients need," said Jason Marx, CEO, Wolters Kluwer Tax & Accounting. "Bringing technology, business transformation, and firm leadership perspectives together helps professionals make informed decisions about where to act now and how to prepare for what comes next."
Key themes from the discussion:
-
AI is a business transformation opportunity, not simply a productivity tool. Panelists challenged firms to define the client outcomes and operating models they will need in the years ahead, then determine where AI can best enable them, instead of using the technology to simply automate today's processes.
-
Successful transformation requires changes in how firms develop people and organize work. As AI takes on more foundational tasks, firms need to consider how newer professionals will build expertise and judgment, and how training, supervision, team structures, and incentives should evolve.
-
Trust and governance will determine how far and how quickly AI can advance. As AI takes on more autonomous work, organizations need clear standards for evidence, accountability, and human oversight, including an understanding of when an AI agent should stop and defer to professional judgment. "Building an agent isn't the challenge. The challenge is integrating agents into business workflows with the right context, governance, and human judgment," said Lara Rubbelke, CTO and Vice President, Frontier Industry Advisory, Microsoft.
-
Firms should start small, measure results, and learn quickly. Value starts with deciding what outcome to drive, such as customer experience, employee productivity, or faster ROI. Anu Saha, SVP and COO, Agentforce, Salesforce urged firms to begin with one workflow and secure the data within it, noting that data transformation doesn't have to start with all of a firm's data at one time. Rather than waiting for every aspect of AI transformation to be resolved, panelists encouraged leaders to establish a small team, define how success will be measured, and use those lessons to guide where and how to scale.
-
New ways of working require a plan, and the investment to back it. Sandra Wiley, CEO, Sandra Wiley

The selloff came after the company reported strong third-quarter results but issued a weaker-than-expected revenue forecast for the current quarter.
Reddit built much of its business around people discovering its discussions through Google searches, and those visitors are increasingly finding answers without ever clicking through to the platform. That puts pressure on the advertising business that has helped turn Reddit into one of the internet's fastest-growing publicly traded companies.
Reddit's third-quarter numbers initially looked healthy. Revenue climbed 53% year over year to $895 million, advertising revenue increased 54% to $847 million, and net income reached $283 million. In the U.S., the number actually fell 2% to 50.7 million, giving investors another reason to question whether the platform can maintain its growth.
Huffman delivered the warning during Thursday's earnings call, explaining that Google search referrals had fallen by more than one million on average every week during October, with the decline accelerating toward the end of the third quarter. Huffman pointed directly at Google's AI Overviews and AI Mode, features that generate answers and summaries directly inside search results. Rather than sending users to websites to find information, Google increasingly gives them what they are looking for on its own page, pushing traditional search links further down.

On Sunday, November 1, nearly 60,000 runners taking on the New York City Marathon will get the rare privilege of having city traffic stop for them as they cover 26.2 miles through the five boroughs. This year also marks 50 years since the race moved beyond its original Central Park loops in 1976, expanding into the citywide event we know today.
There's a lot to keep up with, from the professional races and returning champions to a surprisingly large number of celebrities attempting 26.2 miles. And with coverage stretching from early morning into Sunday night, you don't necessarily have to be standing along First Avenue or waiting near Central Park to catch everyone in action.
Here's what you need to know about watching the race, including start times, broadcasts, and how to follow individual runners.
What Time Does the 2026 NYC Marathon Start?
Things get going at 8 a.m. ET with the men's professional wheelchair division, followed by the women's wheelchair racers at 8:02 a.m. Handcycles and select athletes with disabilities start at 8:22 a.m., before the professional women take off at 8:35 a.m. and the men follow at 9:05 a.m.
The rest of the field will leave Staten Island in five waves, beginning at 9:10 a.m. and continuing through 11:30 a.m.
How to Watch the 2026 NYC Marathon
The main national broadcast starts at 8 a.m. ET on ESPN2, with coverage running until 11:30 a.m. If you'd rather stream, the ESPN app has the same coverage with an ESPN Unlimited plan, plus an extra hour of prerace programming beginning at 7 a.m. and more action through 1 p.m. There's a Spanish-language feed during the main 8 to 11:30 a.m. window as well.
In New York and the surrounding tri-state area, ABC7/WABC-TV is another option. Coverage begins at 7 a.m., ahead of the race broadcast from 8 a.m. to 1 p.m., which you can also stream on the ABC 7 New York app.
For anyone more interested in the finish line than the rest of the course, ABC7NY.com and the ABC 7 New York app have you covered from 10:30 a.m. until 6 p.m. with a dedicated live stream. That should give you plenty of time to catch the professionals and stick around for the thousands of other runners making their way into Central Park.
ABC also has a national Live from the TCS New York City Marathon special scheduled for 3 to 5 p.m. Later that evening, NYRR is giving the final finishers their own broadcast from 8 to 10 p.m. on ABC7NY.com and its YouTube channel. The celebrations don't have to end just because the fastest runners finished hours earlier.
How to Track Runners
Planning to cheer for someone in Brooklyn and then catch them again in Manhattan? Before hopping on the subway, you'll probably want to check how far along they are, which is where the official New York Road Runners app comes in handy.
You can track individual runners throughout the race, check their progress at timing points, and pull up leaderboards and results. The app is available for iOS and Android, and it also has live feeds for each of the four professional races if you want to keep an eye on the elites while you're out cheering.
Who to Watch at the 2026 NYC Marathon
Last year's champions, Benson Kipruto and Hellen Obiri, are both coming back, and each has a memorable performance to defend. Kipruto won the closest men's finish in NYC Marathon history in 2025, while Obiri ran 2:19:51 to break the women's course record that had stood for 22 years.
Conner Mantz and Zouhair Talbi are among the Americans to watch in the men's race.

Missouri’s first report on the academic performance of students in its MOScholars voucher program found encouraging test scores but also exposed gaps in how the state collected the data, including information required by law that remains unavailable.
The report, released Wednesday by the Missouri Treasurer’s Office, found that students scored near the national average in reading and math during the program’s first three years. But researchers could validate test results for only 77% of students in testing grades, and the report lacked information about family income that state law requires.
The findings offer a baseline for measuring student performance but do not establish whether the program has improved academic outcomes or whether its students outperform those in public schools.
Researchers contracted to compile the report say they have an encouraging baseline to build on in future years. But the findings fall short of what some lawmakers expected from a program that has been operating for four years.
The law passed in 2021 that created the MOScholars program requires the state treasurer to “provide the test results and associated learning gains to the public via a state website after the third year of test and test-related data collection.”
Many expected this report last summer, immediately after the program’s third school year. When The Independent asked about the timing in April, the treasurer’s former chief of staff, Jackson Bailey, said the 2025-26 school year was “the fourth year of the MOScholars program, but is the third year of test and test-related data collection.” He said data for each school year is not collected until the following year.

Ahead of the Chicago Marathon, Clayton Young shared that he tore his hamstring, but still planned to compete. One of the strategies he said he used to get to the starting line and, ultimately, to the finish line as the first American: abandoning stretching in lieu of strength work—namely, isometric exercises.
When I heard this, I realized I had something in common with Young. My physical therapist, James Chung, PT, DPT, a sports performance physical therapist based in New York City, also recommends doing isometric strength exercises to deal with tendon issues, including my Achilles tendinopathy.
Isometrics are, indeed, great for pretty much everyone, says Mandy Fox, DPT, a physical therapist for runners in New York City. “An isometric exercise is a muscle contraction where the muscle produces force, but it doesn't change length and the joint angle doesn’t change,” Fox explains.
Basically, you’re loading the muscle and then holding it in one position for a set amount of time, like 30 seconds, as you would do in, say, a plank hold. This is in contrast to a concentric exercise, like lifting weights up to the top of a biceps curl, or an eccentric exercise, like slowly lowering heels down in a calf raise.
Whether you’re dealing with a hamstring tendon issue like Clayton, an Achilles tendon issue like me, or even a hip/glute tendon issue, this type of exercise can help. “This works because across the board, whether you’re elite or amateur, tendons respond to load, but they don’t respond to lengthening,” Fox says, adding that doing isometrics helps you keep running when you’re dealing with tendon issues.
While it’s always best to get evaluated by a doctor or physical therapist to rule out other factors that require a different approach, you can see a few common clues below that might point to a tendon-related injury and how isometrics can help.
In fact, even if you’re totally healthy (enjoy it!), these exercises still offer benefits, says Chung. Here’s how they work in the defense against running injuries, plus specific exercises to try, and how to add them to your routine.
How to Know If You’re Dealing With a Tendon Issue
For one, tendon pain is typically closer to where the joints are, says Chung, so you may feel Achilles tendon pain closer to the ankle and hamstring tendon issues at the sit bone or either side of the knee.
On the other hand, you’ll typically feel muscle strains or tears where the muscle contracts (and you feel pain when that happens). For example, with a calf strain, you might feel it most when you push off the ground, or with a hamstring strain, you might feel it most when your knee extends during the late swing phase of the gait cycle. You will also feel pain when you stretch a strained muscle.
Another way to tell: “Tendon pain is kind of dull and achy depending on what stage you’re in, but tendons will have what’s called a warmup effect where you’ll actually feel better when you warm it up,” Chung says, like after your first mile or two.
